course.title: AP U.S. History
course.description: Trace how Americans have argued over identity, power, work, and their place in the world, from the societies that existed before 1491 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Follow the nation's development from early contact and colonization through independence, civil war, industrialization, world wars, and recent decades.

unit.title: Period 4
unit.description: Follow the rise of party politics and a more participatory democracy, the market revolution, westward expansion and foreign policy, the Second Great Awakening and reform, and the growth of slavery from 1800 to 1848.

firstTopic.title: Contextualizing Period 4
firstTopic.summary: The context for Period 4: a more participatory democracy and a new national culture, an economy transformed by innovation, and a nation that expanded westward and argued over slavery, 1800–1848.

writingQuizzes.title: LEQ: Did economic change create a national identity?

topic.title: America on the World Stage
topic.summary: How the War of 1812, border agreements with Britain and Spain, and the Monroe Doctrine expressed a growing American effort to claim territory, protect trade, and assert influence in the Western Hemisphere.

framework.name: Course themes
framework.title: Use the course themes to choose your evidence
framework.intro: The themes connect developments across all nine periods. A piece of evidence can fit more than one theme; choose the one that answers the prompt.
framework.sourceNote: Theme names, codes, and descriptions follow the AP U.S. History Course and Exam Description (fall 2026).

themes.title: American and National Identity
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why definitions of American and national identity and values have developed among the diverse and changing population of North America as well as on related topics, such as citizenship, constitutionalism, foreign policy, assimilation, and American exceptionalism.
themes.question: Who counted as American, and what did people believe the nation stood for?
themes.example: Debates over ratifying the Constitution turned on what kind of republic Americans wanted.

themes.title: Work, Exchange, and Technology
themes.description: This theme focuses on the factors behind the development of systems of economic exchange, particularly the role of technology, economic markets, and government.
themes.question: How did people earn a living, trade, and use new technology?
themes.example: Canals and railroads tied farmers in the West to markets in the East.

themes.title: Geography and the Environment
themes.description: This theme focuses on the role of geography and both the natural and human-made environments in the social and political developments in what would become the United States.
themes.question: How did land, climate, and resources shape choices, and how did people change them?
themes.example: The Chesapeake's climate suited tobacco, which shaped its labor system.

themes.title: Migration and Settlement
themes.description: This theme focuses on why and how the various people who moved to and within the United States both adapted to and transformed their new social and physical environments.
themes.question: Why did people move, and how did they change the places they settled?
themes.example: The Great Migration brought African Americans from the rural South to northern cities.

themes.title: Politics and Power
themes.description: This theme focuses on how different social and political groups have influenced society and government in the United States as well as how political beliefs and institutions have changed over time.
themes.question: Who held power, how did they use it, and who challenged it?
themes.example: The New Deal expanded the federal government's role in the economy.

themes.title: America in the World
themes.description: This theme focuses on the interactions between nations that affected North American history in the colonial period and on the influence of the United States on world affairs.
themes.question: How did contact, trade, diplomacy, and war connect America to other nations?
themes.example: The Seven Years' War left Britain in debt and changed its policies toward the colonies.

themes.title: American and Regional Culture
themes.description: This theme focuses on the how and why national, regional, and group cultures developed and changed as well as how culture has shaped government policy and the economy.
themes.question: How did beliefs, religion, arts, and media develop and shape public life?
themes.example: The Second Great Awakening inspired many Americans to join reform movements.

themes.title: Social Structures
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why systems of social organization develop and change as well as the impact that these systems have on the broader society.
themes.question: How were people ranked by race, class, and gender, and how did that change?
themes.example: The growth of a middle class in the Gilded Age changed ideas about leisure and family.

questions.prompt: Which of the following was a cause of the War of 1812?
choices: Spain's refusal to sell Florida to the United States after the Louisiana Purchase
British impressment of American sailors and interference with American trade
A French attack on American ports along the Atlantic coast in the summer of 1812
A British plan to take the Louisiana Territory from the United States by force
questions.explanation: Britain seized sailors and ships during its wars with France, and many Americans also blamed Britain for aiding Native resistance in the West.
choiceExplanations: Florida was transferred in 1819, and Spain was not the opponent in 1812.
Britain seized sailors and ships during its wars with France, and many Americans also blamed Britain for aiding Native resistance in the West.
The war was fought against Britain.
Britain had not claimed Louisiana.
questions.distinguisher: The Florida choice is close because Florida was a diplomatic issue in these years, but the war was fought over British actions.
questions.subskillText: Identify a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: The Treaty of Ghent (1814) ended the War of 1812 by
choices: requiring Britain to stop impressing American sailors and to pay for damage to shipping
giving Canada to the United States in exchange for an end of the British blockade
restoring the borders and conditions that had existed before the war began
dividing the Northwest Territory between the British and the Native confederacy
questions.explanation: Neither side won territory, and the treaty restored the conditions before the war.
choiceExplanations: The treaty did not mention impressment or damages.
The treaty did not transfer Canada.
Neither side won territory, and the treaty restored the conditions before the war.
No such division was made.
questions.distinguisher: The impressment choice is close because impressment was a cause of the war, but the treaty did not address it.
questions.subskillText: Explain a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following was an effect of the War of 1812 on American politics?
choices: The Federalist Party declined after its Hartford Convention seemed disloyal
The Federalist Party gained power in Congress by supporting the war effort
The Democratic-Republican Party broke apart and was replaced by a party of war veterans
Congress ended political parties by passing a constitutional amendment in 1815
questions.explanation: Federalists had opposed the war, and their Hartford Convention was widely viewed as unpatriotic, which left the party weak.
choiceExplanations: Federalists had opposed the war, and their Hartford Convention was widely viewed as unpatriotic, which left the party weak.
The Federalists had opposed the war.
The Democratic-Republicans dominated afterward.
No amendment ended parties.
questions.distinguisher: The gain-power choice is close because the party was strong in New England before the war, but its antiwar stance hurt it.
questions.subskillText: Explain a historical concept, development, or process.

choices: added the Oregon Country to the United States and fixed the border with Canada
ended Spanish rule in Mexico and recognized the independence of its provinces
gave Spain control of the Mississippi River in return for the use of New Orleans
transferred Florida from Spain to the United States and extended a boundary to the Pacific
questions.explanation: Spain gave up Florida and accepted a boundary that gave the United States a claim to the Pacific coast.
choiceExplanations: The Oregon boundary was settled in 1846.
Mexico gained independence in 1821 through its own revolution.
Spain gave up claims, and the treaty did not return the Mississippi.
Spain gave up Florida and accepted a boundary that gave the United States a claim to the Pacific coast.
questions.distinguisher: The Oregon choice is close because the treaty touched the Pacific, but the Oregon dispute was settled with Britain later.
questions.subskillText: Identify a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: In the Monroe Doctrine, the United States declared that
choices: it would form an alliance with Britain to defend the new nations of Latin America
it would oppose European efforts to extend their political systems into the Western Hemisphere
it would take control of the existing European colonies in the Western Hemisphere
it would enter European wars whenever democracies were threatened by monarchies
questions.explanation: Monroe warned European powers not to extend their systems to the Americas and promised that the United States would stay out of Europe's wars.
choiceExplanations: The United States acted on its own and not in an alliance with Britain.
Monroe warned European powers not to extend their systems to the Americas and promised that the United States would stay out of Europe's wars.
Monroe said the United States would not interfere with existing colonies.
Monroe said the United States would stay out of European wars.
questions.distinguisher: The Britain alliance choice is close because Britain had proposed a joint statement, but Adams persuaded Monroe to act alone.
questions.subskillText: Identify a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best explains why the United States issued the Monroe Doctrine in 1823?
choices: The United States wanted to annex the new nations of Latin America as new states
Britain had declared war on the United States to win control of the Caribbean
European monarchies discussed helping Spain regain its Latin American colonies
Congress had demanded that the navy build a base on the island of Cuba
questions.explanation: Most of Spain's colonies had won independence, and the United States wanted to keep European monarchies from regaining them.
choiceExplanations: The Doctrine concerned European intervention, not annexation.
Britain and the United States were not at war.
Most of Spain's colonies had won independence, and the United States wanted to keep European monarchies from regaining them.
No such demand drove the Doctrine.
questions.distinguisher: The annexation choice is close because American expansion was a theme of the period, but the Doctrine defended independence.
questions.subskillText: Explain how a historical development or process relates to another historical development or process.

questions.prompt: The Rush–Bagot Agreement (1817) and the Convention of 1818 are best understood in the context of which of the following?
choices: A postwar effort to settle disputes with Britain peacefully
A preparation for a second war with Britain over the borders of Canada
An American effort to annex British Canada through a treaty with Parliament
The need to end the Embargo Act, which had closed American ports in 1807
questions.explanation: After the war, both nations chose to limit naval forces on the Great Lakes and fix the northern boundary.
choiceExplanations: After the war, both nations chose to limit naval forces on the Great Lakes and fix the northern boundary.
The agreements reduced the danger of conflict.
The agreements did not transfer Canada.
The embargo had ended in 1809.
questions.distinguisher: The second war choice is close because the agreements followed a war, but they lowered tensions.
questions.subskillText: Identify and describe a historical context for a specific historical development or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following reflects a continuity in United States foreign policy from Washington's presidency to the Monroe Doctrine?
choices: A commitment to join Britain or France whenever either went to war
A wish to avoid entanglement in European political conflicts
A refusal to claim new territory in North America or in the Caribbean
An unwillingness to defend American trade with force
questions.explanation: Washington's Farewell Address and Monroe's message both urged the nation to stay out of Europe's quarrels.
choiceExplanations: American leaders chose neutrality and not commitments to join either power.
Washington's Farewell Address and Monroe's message both urged the nation to stay out of Europe's quarrels.
The nation claimed more territory over time.
The United States used force when it saw its trade threatened, as in 1812.
questions.distinguisher: The join-either-power choice is close because the nation had treaties with France, but leaders later avoided such commitments.
questions.subskillText: Identify patterns among or connections between historical developments and processes.

questions.prompt: Which of the following was Monroe's primary purpose in the second paragraph of the excerpt?
choices: To ask Britain for an alliance against the European monarchies that wished to restore Spain's rule
To declare that the United States would take possession of the remaining European colonies
To warn European powers against extending their systems to independent nations in the hemisphere
To announce that the United States would send troops to defend the new nations in battle
questions.explanation: Monroe says that any European attempt to oppress or control the independent governments would be viewed as unfriendly to the United States.
choiceExplanations: Monroe announced a policy that the United States would follow on its own.
He said the United States would not interfere with existing colonies.
Monroe says that any European attempt to oppress or control the independent governments would be viewed as unfriendly to the United States.
He did not promise troops.
questions.distinguisher: The alliance choice is close because Britain had proposed joint action, but the excerpt shows a unilateral warning.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 4.4, KC-4.3.I.A.ii: the U.S. government sought influence and control over the Western Hemisphere through a variety of means, including diplomatic efforts such as the Monroe Doctrine
stimulusBlocks.attribution: President James Monroe, in his annual message to Congress, December 2, 1823, after Spain's American colonies had won independence and European monarchies had talked of restoring royal rule
stimulusBlocks.citation: James Monroe, Seventh Annual Message to Congress (December 2, 1823), in State of the Union Addresses of James Monroe. Project Gutenberg eBook #5014.
stimulusBlocks.note: “The allied powers” are the monarchies of Europe, especially the Holy Alliance of Russia, Austria, and Prussia. “This hemisphere” is the Western Hemisphere.
stimulusBlocks.text:
In the wars of the European powers in matters relating to themselves we have never taken any part, nor does it comport with our policy so to do.

We owe it, therefore, to candor and to the amicable relations existing between the United States and those powers to declare that we should consider any attempt on their part to extend their system to any portion of this hemisphere as dangerous to our peace and safety. With the existing colonies or dependencies of any European power we have not interfered and shall not interfere, but with the Governments who have declared their independence and maintained it, and whose independence we have, on great consideration and on just principles, acknowledged, we could not view any interposition for the purpose of oppressing them, or controlling in any other manner their destiny, by any European power in any other light than as the manifestation of an unfriendly disposition toward the United States.

questions.subskillText: Explain the point of view, purpose, historical situation, and/or audience of a source.

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements about United States policy is best supported by the excerpt?
choices: The United States would leave existing colonies alone but resist European control of independent nations
The United States would act to remove all European colonies from the Western Hemisphere
The United States regarded the independence of the Latin American nations as a danger
The United States would take part in the wars of Europe to defend the cause of freedom
questions.explanation: Monroe separates existing colonies, which the United States will leave alone, from independent governments, which it will defend against European control.
choiceExplanations: Monroe separates existing colonies, which the United States will leave alone, from independent governments, which it will defend against European control.
Monroe said that the United States had not interfered and would not interfere with existing colonies.
He said the United States had acknowledged their independence on just principles.
The first paragraph states that the United States had never taken part in those wars.
questions.distinguisher: The remove-all-colonies choice is close because the Doctrine opposed new colonization, but it accepted the colonies that already existed.

questions.prompt: Which of the following developments most directly led to the policy that Monroe announces in the excerpt?
choices: The Louisiana Purchase, which had given the United States control of the Mississippi
The independence won by Spain's former colonies and talk of restoring them to Spain
The Treaty of Ghent, which had ended the war and returned the borders of 1812
The Missouri Compromise, which had set the boundary between slave and free territory
questions.explanation: The independence of Latin American nations and the fear of European intervention led the United States to declare its hemispheric policy.
choiceExplanations: That purchase was in 1803 and concerned North American territory.
The independence of Latin American nations and the fear of European intervention led the United States to declare its hemispheric policy.
The treaty settled the war with Britain, and the Doctrine concerned Latin America.
That compromise concerned slavery and not European colonies.
questions.distinguisher: The Louisiana choice is close because it also expanded American influence, but the Doctrine responded to events in Latin America.
